V01-J-001: When a school's reputation rests on a single annual examination, teachers face a strong temptation to teach only what that examination is likely to ask. This temptation is understandable, since a teacher whose pupils score poorly may be blamed regardless of what else those pupils have learned. Yet the cost of giving in to it is borne by the pupils, who learn to recognise question formats instead of understanding the subject behind them. Such pupils often do well in the examination hall and then struggle the moment a problem is posed in an unfamiliar form.
V01-J-002: In the middle of the nineteenth century, most London physicians believed that cholera spread through foul air rising from filth and decay. During the outbreak of 1854, however, the physician John Snow traced the homes of the dead and found them clustered around one public water pump. When he persuaded the local authorities to remove the pump's handle, he was acting on his rival view that the disease travelled through contaminated water. The map he later drew of those deaths is remembered less for settling the question at once, which it did not, than for showing how the pattern of cases could itself be evidence.
V01-J-003: For centuries, many European cities were enclosed by thick walls that protected their inhabitants but also confined their growth. As artillery improved and national armies replaced local militias, these fortifications lost most of their military value. Rather than leave them to crumble, several cities demolished their walls and laid out broad ring roads along the line they had occupied. The result is a pattern still visible on modern maps, in which a dense medieval core is circled by a wide boulevard lined with later public buildings.
V01-J-004: Most people overestimate how much others notice their appearance and behaviour, a tendency psychologists call the spotlight effect. Someone who arrives at a party with a stain on a shirt, for instance, may spend the evening convinced that everyone has seen it. In fact, the other guests are largely occupied with their own worries about how they themselves are coming across. Recognising this can be oddly liberating, because it suggests that the audience we imagine judging us is mostly absorbed in its own performance.
V01-J-005: In many communities, the expected cost of a wedding has risen far faster than the incomes of the families who must pay for it. One reason is that a wedding is a public display, and each family's celebration is measured against the most lavish ones its guests have recently attended. Because no family wishes to appear meaner than its neighbours, the standard keeps rising even when most hosts privately wish it would stop. Breaking this cycle therefore requires a shared change in expectations, since a single family that spends modestly only invites comment.
V01-J-006: Teachers have long noticed that pupils return from the long summer holiday having forgotten part of what they learned the previous year. This loss is not spread evenly, however, because children from homes with books, outings and educated parents often hold their ground or even advance. Children without such resources, by contrast, tend to fall back, so that a gap which was small in June has widened by September. Repeated over several summers, these seasonal differences may account for a good share of the gap observed between the two groups by the end of school. If that is so, then some of the inequality usually blamed on schools arises in the months when schools are closed.
V01-J-007: Requiring restaurants to print the calorie content of each dish beside its price seems an obvious way to help diners eat more healthily. The reasoning behind the rule is simple: people choose badly partly because they do not know what their food contains. But diners who already care about calories tend to know roughly what they are ordering, while those who do not care are unlikely to be moved by a number. The labels may therefore change less what customers choose than what restaurants offer, since few chains wish to advertise a dish with an alarming figure.
V01-J-008: Much of what a skilled craftsperson knows cannot be written down, because it lives in the hands and the eye rather than in rules. A master carpenter, for example, can tell from the sound of a plane whether the blade needs sharpening, yet would struggle to explain how. Knowledge of this kind, like the carpenter's ear for a blunt blade, passes from one person to another only through long periods of watching, trying and being corrected. That is why the apprenticeship, slow and costly as it seems, survived for centuries even in trades that had plenty of printed manuals.
V01-J-009: A disease that affects only a few thousand people worldwide offers a drug company little prospect of recovering the cost of developing a treatment. Left to the market alone, such conditions would therefore attract almost no research, however severe the suffering they cause. Several governments have responded by offering firms that develop drugs for rare diseases extended periods of exclusive sale and other incentives. These incentives have worked, perhaps too well, since some companies now charge prices for such drugs that strain even wealthy health systems. The policy has thus traded one problem for another: treatments that once did not exist now exist but are rationed by their cost.
V01-J-010: For decades, the standard response to informal settlements was to clear them and move their residents to new housing on the edge of the city. The new blocks were often sound, but they stood far from the markets, workshops and households where residents had earned their living. Cut off from these sources of income, many families sold or abandoned their allotted flats and drifted back towards the centre. Such failures pushed planners towards upgrading settlements where they stand, laying pipes and paving lanes while leaving the networks of livelihood intact.
V01-J-011: Imagine a machine that could give you any experiences you wished, indistinguishable from real life, for as long as you remained plugged in. If pleasure were the only thing that mattered, we should all be eager to connect ourselves to it for life. Most people, however, recoil from the offer, and the reasons they give are telling: they want actually to do things, not merely to feel that they are doing them. The thought experiment is therefore usually taken as evidence that we value contact with reality for its own sake, and not only for the feelings it produces.
V01-J-012: When people look back on a painful experience, their verdict depends surprisingly little on how long the pain lasted. What they remember instead is chiefly how bad it was at its worst moment and how it felt at the very end. This produces a strange possibility: adding a few minutes of milder discomfort to the end of a procedure can make the whole of it remembered as less unpleasant. Measured minute by minute, of course, the longer procedure contains strictly more suffering than the shorter one. Between them, these two verdicts show that the self who lives through an experience and the self who later remembers it may keep very different accounts.
V01-J-013: Not long ago, a visible tattoo in many societies marked its wearer as belonging to the margins: sailors, prisoners, or members of rough trades. Over a few decades the same marks have migrated to the arms of accountants, teachers and grandmothers, and the old associations have largely faded. Yet the change has not erased the tattoo's power to signal; it has simply altered what is being signalled. Where a tattoo once announced that its wearer stood outside respectable society, it now more often announces a taste, a memory or an attachment the wearer wishes to display.
V01-J-014: Asking pupils to mark one another's work is often defended as a way of saving teachers' time. Its real value lies elsewhere, in what the marker learns by applying the criteria to someone else's attempt. A pupil who has had to decide why a classmate's answer earns only half the marks is far more likely to notice the same weakness in her own. Her judgement is only as sound as her grasp of the criteria, however, so pupils must first be taught what good work looks like, or they will simply reward neatness and length.
V01-J-015: Patients facing a serious diagnosis are often advised to seek a second opinion, on the reasonable ground that any single doctor can be mistaken. The value of that second opinion, however, depends on its independence from the first. A specialist who is shown the original report before examining the patient will tend to see what it describes, and to confirm a diagnosis she might otherwise have questioned. To guard against this anchoring, the new doctor should examine the patient and form a view before reading what the first one concluded.
V01-J-016: City authorities often treat street vendors as an obstruction to be cleared from pavements in the name of order and hygiene. Yet the same vendors supply cheap food and goods to commuters and workers whom formal shops, with their higher rents, do not serve. They also keep streets occupied after offices close, and an occupied street is, by most accounts, a safer one. Clearing them therefore removes services that someone must then replace, often at greater public cost. A wiser policy would regulate where and when vending takes place rather than pretend that the demand it meets can be abolished.
V01-J-017: Resentment is sometimes treated as a mere failing, a refusal to let go that harms the person who feels it more than anyone else. But resentment also carries a judgement: that one has been wronged, and that the wrong matters. This is why forgiveness given too quickly can seem less a virtue than a kind of self-disrespect, as though the injury had not really counted. Genuine forgiveness, then, must avoid that appearance: it acknowledges the wrong fully and only then gives up the resentment the wrong justified.
V01-J-018: In many societies a child takes the father's surname, a custom so familiar that it is easily mistaken for a natural arrangement. Elsewhere, children receive both parents' names, or a name derived from a parent's given name, or no fixed family name at all. The variety suggests that surnames answer social needs, such as tracing inheritance or registering citizens, rather than any fact about families themselves. Seen in that light, disputes over which name a child should carry are less about tradition than about which of those needs a society now considers most important.
V01-J-019: Suppose you had to choose the rules of a society without knowing what place you would occupy in it: your class, talents, sex or health. Unable to favour yourself, you would have to consider how the rules looked from every position, including the worst. Fearing that the worst position might be their own, prudent choosers behind such a veil, it has been argued, would insist that the least advantaged be made as well off as possible. Critics reply that this conclusion owes less to the veil than to an assumed horror of risk, since a chooser willing to gamble might prefer greater rewards at the top. The device, then, does not settle what justice requires by itself, but it does force each side to state openly the attitude to risk on which its answer depends.
V01-J-020: A politician who refuses ever to lie, bargain with scoundrels or break a promise may keep a clean conscience while the people they serve pay for those scruples. Some have concluded that public office simply suspends private morality, so that what would be wrong for a citizen is permitted to a minister. The more troubling view is that the act remains wrong even when it is necessary, so that a good politician must sometimes do wrong and know it. On this account the mark of such a leader is not innocence but the willingness to carry guilt for what the office required.
V01-J-021: Told that a treatment gives ninety out of a hundred patients five more years of life, most people find it attractive. Told that ten out of a hundred will die within five years, many of the same people hesitate, although the two statements describe exactly the same outcome. A tempting conclusion is that people are simply careless with numbers, but the effect has been reported even among doctors who understand that the figures are equivalent. If arithmetic is not what fails, then what the framing alters is not the information people receive but the feature of the situation on which their attention settles.
V01-J-022: People tend to assume that their own opinions and habits are more widely shared than they actually are. Part of the explanation is simply exposure, since we spend our time among people who resemble us and so mistake our circle for the world. But if exposure were the whole story, the bias should vanish once people learn the true figures, and it often seems not to. One likely addition is motive: believing that one's views are common is comforting, because it makes them seem normal and therefore reasonable. A belief that serves such a need is not easily corrected by information, since it was never held merely on the strength of information.
V01-J-023: Rivers seem ideal boundaries, visible to everyone and hard to cross, which is why so many treaties have fixed borders along them. Yet a river is not a line but a process, forever eroding one bank, building up the other and occasionally abandoning its bed altogether. A border drawn along the channel as it ran on the day of signing may within a generation leave fields and villages on the wrong side of the water. Such stranded villages turn the river's chief merit as a frontier, its plain visibility, into a source of dispute, since anyone can see that the water no longer runs where the treaty says.
V01-J-024: A fixed age at which working life ends seems to many people a natural feature of the life course, like adolescence or old age itself. It is in fact a fairly recent invention, which spread with state pension schemes from the late nineteenth century onwards. When those schemes began, the qualifying age was set high enough that relatively few workers could expect to draw a pension for many years. Life expectancy has since risen greatly, but in many countries the qualifying age has risen far less, turning retirement from a brief coda into a long stage of life. Debates about raising that age are therefore not attempts to abolish a timeless right, but disputes over how to adjust an arrangement whose original assumptions no longer hold.
V01-J-025: Money is supposed to be interchangeable: a rupee won in a lottery buys exactly what a rupee earned at work buys. Yet people treat money differently according to where it came from, spending a windfall freely while guarding wages with care. Economic theory long treated such habits as simple errors, a failure to see that the source of a sum makes no difference to its value. On reflection, though, keeping separate mental accounts may be a rough but serviceable defence against temptation, a way of protecting rent money from the lure of a holiday.
